In mathematics, '''Krener's theorem''' is a result attributed to [[Arthur J. Krener]] in geometric [[control theory]] about the topological properties of [[attainable set]]s of finite-dimensional control systems.  It states that any attainable set of a [[bracket-generating]] system has nonempty interior or, equivalently, that any attainable set has nonempty interior in the topology of the corresponding [[orbit (control theory)|orbit]]. Heuristically, Krener's theorem prohibits attainable sets from being [[hairy ball theorem|hairy]].

==Theorem==
Let 
<math>{\ }\dot q=f(q,u)</math> 
be a smooth control system, where 
<math>{\ q}</math> 
belongs to a <!-- <math>\ n</math>- -->finite-dimensional manifold <math>\ M</math> and <math>\ u</math> belongs to a control set <math>\ U</math>. Consider the family  of vector fields <math>{\mathcal F}=\{f(\cdot,u)\mid u\in U\}</math>.

Let <math>\ \mathrm{Lie}\,\mathcal{F}</math> be the [[Lie algebra]] generated by <math>{\mathcal F}</math> with respect to the [[Lie bracket of vector fields]]. 
Given <math>\ q\in M</math>, if the vector space <math>\ \mathrm{Lie}_q\,\mathcal{F}=\{g(q)\mid g\in \mathrm{Lie}\,\mathcal{F}\}</math> is equal to <math>\ T_q M</math>,
then <math>\ q</math> belongs to the closure of the interior of the attainable set from <math>\ q</math>.

==Remarks and consequences==
Even if <math>\mathrm{Lie}_q\,\mathcal{F}</math> is different from <math>\ T_q M</math>,
the attainable set from <math>\ q</math> has nonempty interior in the orbit topology,
as it follows from Krener's theorem applied to the control system restricted to the orbit through <math>\ q</math>.

When all the vector fields in <math>\ \mathcal{F}</math> are analytic,  <math>\ \mathrm{Lie}_q\,\mathcal{F}=T_q M</math> '''if and only if''' <math>\ q</math> belongs to the closure of the interior of the attainable set from <math>\ q</math>. This is a consequence of Krener's theorem and of the [[orbit (control theory)#Orbit theorem (Nagano-Sussmann)|orbit theorem]].

As a corollary of Krener's theorem one can prove that if the system is bracket-generating and if the attainable set from <math>\ q\in M</math> is dense in <math>\ M</math>, then the attainable set from <math>\ q</math>
is actually equal to <math>\ M</math>.
